title: Design the API for a Photo-Sharing App
oneLiner: An API design round, stage by stage: resources, endpoints, uploads, feeds, retries, errors and limits, then compare with a strong answer.
keyTakeaway: An API design round is graded on the contract, not the boxes behind it: clear resources and methods, the right status codes, cursor pagination for anything that scrolls, idempotent writes for anything a mobile client will retry, uploads that go straight to object storage, one error format, and a versioning and auth story. Say the trade-off behind each choice and the failure each one prevents.
explanation:
Some interviews (and many system design rounds at the 4-minute API stage) ask you to design an API rather than a whole system: "Design the public API for an Instagram-like app", "Design the API for a food delivery service", "What would the endpoints for Google Calendar look like?". The interviewer wants to see you think as the owner of a contract that other teams and companies will build against for years. This walk-through practises that with a photo-sharing app used by a mobile client and by third-party developers.

It uses the same format as the system design walk-throughs: the widget gives the prompt and then one stage at a time. Write your own answer in the box first, the way you would say it out loud, and only then compare it with the model answer and tick the points you covered. Your notes stay in this browser.

A good order for an API round: clarify who the clients are and what they need (about 5 minutes); name the resources and their relationships (5); list the endpoints with methods, key fields and status codes (8); handle the hard reads, meaning the feed and pagination (6); handle the hard writes, meaning uploads, likes and retries (8); then errors, versioning and evolution (5); and finally authentication, scopes and rate limits (5). Each stage draws on one lesson in this track, so if a stage goes badly, that lesson is the one to reread.

Habits that score well: write endpoints in a consistent notation (METHOD /path, body, response, status codes), state what is idempotent and how, show a response body for the most important call, and keep asking "what happens when the client retries this?" and "what happens when we need to change this next year?".
